## Simple explanation

A multilayer perceptron (MLP) is a neural network made of layers that pass
information forward. Each layer combines its inputs, applies a learned
transformation, and usually uses a nonlinear activation.

## Technical explanation

An MLP with $L$ layers can be written as:

$$
h^{(0)} = x,\qquad
h^{(\ell)} = \phi\left(W^{(\ell)}h^{(\ell-1)} + b^{(\ell)}\right)
$$

where $W^{(\ell)}$ and $b^{(\ell)}$ are learned parameters and $\phi$ is a
nonlinear activation. The output layer may use a task-specific transformation
or activation. Without nonlinear activations, stacking linear layers is
equivalent to a single linear transformation.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

MLPs are a fundamental neural-network building block and can model nonlinear
relationships. They are used for tabular data, prediction heads, and
feed-forward sublayers inside larger architectures, including Transformers.

## How it works

The input passes through successive dense layers. Training compares the
output with target data using a loss and updates the weights through
backpropagation. Layer width, depth, activation, regularization, and data
preparation all affect performance.

## Practical example

An MLP can classify a record from numeric features such as age, account
activity, and transaction amount. Hidden layers learn combinations of those
features, and an output layer estimates class scores.

## Common misconceptions

- More layers or neurons do not guarantee better generalization.
- An MLP does not automatically understand spatial or sequential structure; other architectures or input representations may be better suited.
- An MLP with only linear transformations cannot represent nonlinear functions.
